title: Mueller residents upset after self-driving car runs over, kills duck

reading.body:
A self-driving car operated by Avride struck and killed a duck in a residential neighborhood in Austin, Texas. The vehicle was in autonomous mode with a human safety operator present but did not slow down or attempt to avoid the animal. This shows a perception or decision-making failure in which the system either did not detect the duck or did not classify it as an obstacle requiring avoidance.

A resident claimed the vehicle had also failed to stop at a stop sign, though Avride disputed this after reviewing its data and said the vehicle had made appropriate stops. Whether the perception failure was specific to the duck or part of a broader detection problem is not established. The incident prompted the company to exclude certain streets from its service area and to run simulations to evaluate potential improvements, suggesting the system was deployed in conditions without sufficient testing for small obstacles in residential zones.

Mueller residents upset after self-driving car runs over, kills duck

summary:
An autonomous vehicle operated by Avride struck and killed a mother duck in the Mueller Lake neighborhood of Austin, Texas, prompting significant community backlash. The incident occurred when the self-driving car, which had a human safety operator present, hit the duck without slowing down or stopping. The duck was well-known to residents because it had been nesting in a pot outside a local Italian restaurant, which intensified neighborhood concerns about autonomous vehicle safety in residential areas.

Avride confirmed the vehicle was operating in autonomous mode at the time of the incident. The company has since adjusted its testing operations by excluding certain streets around the lake from its service area. A resident claimed the vehicle failed to stop at a stop sign, but Avride disputed this after reviewing vehicle data and simulation replays, stating the car made appropriate stops. The company is now running controlled simulation experiments to evaluate potential technology improvements that could prevent similar situations while maintaining safety performance.
